idiom_name: class Orders over a private std::vector<Order>, std::span<const Order> for reads
implementation_notes: The standard library supplies a generic container, not a domain collection: keep std::vector<Order> (or std::deque/std::set when the invariants want it) as a private member and write the class yourself - validating mutators, [[nodiscard]] accessors, and read exposure that cannot mutate the container. std::span<const Order> is the modern answer to 'return the collection without giving it away' (C++20): it accepts vectors, arrays and subranges, so callers do not have to build a vector to read, and std::span<const T> documents read-only intent at element level, unlike a const span. Pre-C++20 code returns const std::vector<Order>& instead. Element-type constraints (template <std::same_as<Order>> or a concept) are optional; the reason this class exists is the invariants, not the element type.
pitfalls: Returning a reference or pointer to the vector, or a mutable span, re-opens the container; prefer std::span<const Order> or a const reference.
A span does not own anything: a view taken from a temporary, or held across a reallocating mutation, dangles - document the lifetime as valid until the next mutation.
The container's iterator-invalidation rules become part of your API contract: push_back can invalidate spans and iterators handed out earlier.
Inheriting from std::vector (or any standard container) is legal but wrong here: it publishes every mutating method and the invariants go with it; wrap instead.
